It was extensive that current research on the celadon of the Guan kiln from the Southern Song Dynasty. In terms of its raw materials and processes, the studies pointed out that the Guan body was composed of iron-rich Zijin clay and other local clay, while local clay, limestone, and plant ash were applied to make glaze8,9,10,11,12,13, which was fired at a reduced atmosphere of about 1220 °C14,15,16. Thus, the Guan porcelain showed a stable chemical composition in the glaze, characterized by low SiO2, high Al2O3, and high content of alkali and alkaline-earth metal oxide17,18,19,20,21,22,23. Specifically, the high iron content resulted dark body, while the iron oxide in the glaze was only about 1%24,25. Besides, detailed analyses indicated that celadon coloration was controlled by Fe2+, Fe3+, and a nano-scale phase-separation structure, with micro-sized bubbles and crystals enhancing the opacifying texture17,19,26,27. For glaze decoration, the glaze cracks owing to the difference in the thermal expansion coefficient between the glaze and body, and its replication method was revealed by Ye et al.28,29. Previous studies have mostly focused on the analysis of the single characteristics of the glaze surface for the Guan kiln celadon, but comprehensive research is still weak.
This work was comprehensive and systematically revealed the formation mechanism of color, opacifying, and cracks on the glaze surface of the celadons from the Southern Song Guan kiln, by integrating analyses of physicochemical composition, iron occurrence form, microstructure, and thermal property. In these basics, we further explored the different possibilities for the influencing factors of its characteristic blue hue. Although phase-separated droplets were present, their sizes (<30 nm) fall below the regime where Rayleigh or Mie scattering becomes optically significant, and therefore they do not directly generate structural color. This differs from the mechanism responsible for the pronounced structural blue of most celadon (such as Ru ware), where droplet sizes typically match optical scattering scales19,20,24,25,30,31. In the present glazes, the nanoscale droplets are more consequential due to their compositional partitioning. Their formation promotes the preferential incorporation of Fe together with Ca, Mg, and P into the same separated domains, leading to localized enrichment or segregation of Fe species. This redistribution enhances the chromatic depth of Guan-kiln celadon by modifying the local ligand field and short-range order of Fe-bearing units. Additionally, although the droplet size is too small to generate structural coloration, sub-wavelength scattering from these nanodomains still contributes subtly to the jade-like, translucent texture characteristic of high-quality Guan-kiln glazes42.
The glaze of the Southern Song Guan kiln celadon, owing to its high-viscosity glaze formula and a thick glazing process, as shown in Fig. 9, became opacifying. This was primarily attributed to the combined effects of abundant bubbles and nanoscale phase-separated droplets. The bubbles prolonged the light path through multiple refractions and reflections, while the droplets contributed significantly through Rayleigh scattering. Although crystals also participate in light scattering, their influence was secondary due to their low concentration and angle-dependent optical properties.

The mechanisms of color, opacifying, and cracks in celadon glazes from the Southern Song Guan Kiln
Download PDF
Download PDF
Abstract
Guan ware celadon from the Southern Song Dynasty is renowned for its distinctive glaze appearance. This study applied a multi-technique analysis to systematically integrate the chemical composition, iron occurrence form, physical structure, microscopic morphology, and thermal property, explaining the formation mechanism of color, opacifying, and cracks for Guan ware celadon. The result indicated that some glazes were dominated by chemical coloring (the structure of the chromogenic coordination group about iron), influenced by K2O, CaO, and the firing atmosphere. The opacifying resulted from the increase in the light scattering path, which was due to the crystals, abundant bubbles caused by the calcium-alkali type and thick glaze processes, and the structure of nanoscale phase separation. The cracks were mainly attributable to the bigger coefficient of thermal expansion in the glaze, associated with its composition (higher CaO, lower Al2O3). Moreover, the stress effect was further amplified by the thin body and thick glaze.

Introduction
Celadon, with its long history and wide use, holds a central position in the history of Chinese ceramics, distinguished by its blue-green color and distinctive jade-like quality, which is achieved through the careful control of iron content and the reduction atmosphere during firing. In particular, Guan kiln is outstanding in the firing of celadon. The Guan kiln, one of the “Five Great Kilns of the Song dynasty”, produced celadon ware representing the superior technique of court-used ceramics in Chinese history. Quartz and silicon oxides were commonly found in the glaze, mostly as unmelted residues of raw materials. Under the force of high temperature (the firing temperature of Guan kiln was usually ~1220 °C), due to the high K2O content in the glaze, some SiO2 was stably transformed into tridymite38,39. Obviously, the glaze of G-5 contained the highest amount of fluxing oxides (CaO, MgO, K2O, Na2O) and the lowest content of refractory oxides (SiO2 and Al2O3), resulting in a relatively lower melting temperature of the glaze. Therefore, in the crystal transformation of quartz, tridymite was earliest crystallize and was maintained. At the same time, the high CaO content of the glaze directly contributed to the growth of anorthite crystals.
Besides, the crystal distribution characteristics and formation mechanism of the glaze surface for celadon were further explained from their microstructure. SEM observation (Fig. 6b) showed that there were densely distributed structures like bubbles in the glaze layer, with the highest distribution in G-3, G-4, and G-5. For G-3, block-shaped crystals were found inside the bubbles at high magnification, and combined with EDS elemental composition, it was confirmed to be quartz crystals (Fig. S2). At high temperatures, due to heterogeneous nucleation, which occurred during the melting process of glaze raw materials, the element of Si was rich near quartz crystals, and the solubility of H2O, SO2, and O2 was reduced in the local melt. After gas supersaturation, new bubbles were continuously formed, resulting in bubble aggregation around the quartz crystal40. Due to the highest SiO2 content in G-3, during the firing process, the gas in its glaze melt was relatively more prone to supersaturation and the formation of bubbles near quartz.
The bubbles in the glaze layer can also enhance the opacifying effect of the glaze. As shown in Fig. 7, analyzing the size distribution of bubbles per unit area (200 bubbles) indicated that the bubbles in samples G-1, G-2, and G-3 were bigger and had a higher distribution density, whereas the bubbles in samples G-4, G-5, and G-6 showed opposite features. For G-3, block-shaped crystals were found inside the bubbles at high magnification, and combined with EDS elemental composition, it was confirmed to be quartz crystals (Fig. S2). At high temperatures, due to heterogeneous nucleation, which occurred during the melting process of glaze raw materials, the element of Si was rich near quartz crystals, and the solubility of H2O, SO2, and O2 was reduced in the local melt. After gas supersaturation, new bubbles were continuously formed, resulting in bubble aggregation around the quartz crystal40. Due to the highest SiO2 content in G-3, during the firing process, the gas in its glaze melt was relatively more prone to supersaturation and the formation of bubbles near quartz.
The bubbles in the glaze layer can also enhance the opacifying effect of the glaze. As shown in Fig. 7, analyzing the size distribution of bubbles per unit area (200 bubbles) indicated that the bubbles in samples G-1, G-2, and G-3 were bigger and had a higher distribution density, whereas the bubbles in samples G-4, G-5, and G-6 showed opposite features. This large number of bubbles with varying sizes increased the path of light scattering to decrease the transparency of the glaze layer. Especially the larger and more dense the bubbles, the stronger the opacifying effect41. The difference in bubble size and density may be related to the influence of fusant viscosity at high temperatures, caused by the chemical composition of the glaze. G-1, G-2, and G-3 had less CaO and K2O introduced from limestone raw material, and more SiO2 compared to G-4, G-5, and G-6. Therefore, under the same firing conditions, the higher viscosity resulted in the gas being difficult to escape from the glaze layer, forming the big bubbles30,42. When light shone on the glaze layer, due to the difference in refractive index between the glass phase, crystals, and bubbles, the light was repeatedly scattered in these phases, and could not directly pass through, resulting in an opaque and jade-like texture of glaze.

Moreover, an ultraviolet-visible-near infrared absorption spectrometer (UV-vis-NIR) was analyzed by a Cary 7000 spectrometer, using an integrating sphere test to obtain absorption spectra of the sample glaze surfaces, with a wavelength range of 200–2300 nm. The size of G-6 was too small to meet the testing conditions.
Phase identifications of the glaze surface for all samples were obtained by a D/max-2200 PC X-ray diffraction (XRD, from Japan), whose test depth was 10 µm, the voltage was 40 kV, the tube current was 30 mA, the scanning speed was 1.2 °/min, and the scanning range was 5–75°. Before testing, it needed to cut the samples into 5 × 5 × 3 mm-sized blocks, then ultrasonically clean and dry them. Besides, the vibration peak of carbon in the glazes was measured by using a confocal laser Raman spectrometer (Renishaw-Invia, UK), which was excited by a 532 nm solid-state exciter. The laser power was 1 mW, the collection time of each spectrum was 60 s, and the range was 100–2000 cm-1.
The bubbles and cracks in the glaze surface were observed by optical microscopy (OM, VHX-5000, Japan) under circular illumination. Moreover, comparing the crystals and phase-separated structure of each sample was performed using a scanning electron microscope (SEM, Hitachi S-4800) and energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS, AMETEK EDAX). Before testing the SEM, samples should be etched with 1 vol% HF for 30 s to remove the glass phase from the glaze, then cleaned and dried.
Results
As shown in Fig. 3a, the L* value of celadon glaze from the Southern Song Guan kiln was at 60 ± 10, indicating that the glaze surface had moderate and stable brightness characteristics. The a* ranged from −8.49 to −2.25, and the b* value ranged to 2.56–8.99. The synergistic effect of the two formed a glaze color tone dominated by yellow-green. Besides, all of C* were below 10, showing a typical low saturation. h° corresponded to the reflection peak position in Fig. 3b, which indicated that the G-4 and G-5 obtained the yellow color, G-1 and G-6 were green, while G-2 and G-3 appeared blue tendency.

This work was comprehensive and systematically revealed the formation mechanism of color, opacifying, and cracks on the glaze surface of the celadons from the Southern Song Guan kiln, by integrating analyses of physicochemical composition, iron occurrence form, microstructure, and thermal property. Methods
The celadon samples examined in this study were excavated from the Southern Song Dynasty Guan kiln site at the Jiaotanxia and provided by Zhejiang University. Six specimens (designated G-1 to G-6, Fig. 2 and Table 1) were analyzed. These samples exhibited variations in body color, glaze thickness, and crack patterns, offering representative insights into the kiln’s technological practices. Although the sample size was relatively small—a common constraint in archaeological studies—the selected pieces encompassed the primary visual and microstructural characteristics typical of Southern Song Guan ware, thereby enabling meaningful technological interpretation.
